title: How does the stock market work?
seoTitle: How the Stock Market Works: Shares, Exchanges and Prices Explained
seoDescription: Learn what shares represent, how exchanges and brokers work, why stock prices move, and what investors should understand about risk and valuation.
excerpt: The stock market connects companies that issue ownership shares with investors who buy and sell those shares through organized markets.
author: KitsuWire Editorial
keyTakeaways: A share represents an ownership interest in a company.
Primary markets raise capital for companies; secondary markets let investors trade existing shares.
Prices move as buyers and sellers continuously reassess expected profits, risks and valuations.
Short-term price movements can be noisy, while long-term returns are closely tied to business performance and the price paid for that performance.
body: The stock market is a system for issuing and trading ownership in public companies. When you buy a share, you acquire a small economic interest in the company, although the exact voting and economic rights depend on the share class.
Modern markets connect investors through brokers, exchanges and electronic trading systems that continuously match buyers and sellers.

sections.heading: Primary market vs secondary market
paragraphs: When a company first sells shares to raise capital, the transaction happens in the primary market. An initial public offering is one well-known example.
After shares are issued, investors trade them with each other in the secondary market. Most daily stock-market activity is secondary-market trading rather than money flowing directly to the company.

sections.heading: What exchanges do
paragraphs: Stock exchanges provide organized venues and rules for trading listed securities. They establish listing standards, publish market data and support systems that match orders.
Not every trade happens on a traditional exchange, but exchanges remain central to price discovery and market infrastructure.

sections.heading: How brokers connect investors to the market
paragraphs: Most individual investors do not send orders directly to an exchange. A broker receives the order and routes it to an execution venue.
Different order types affect execution. A market order prioritizes immediate execution, while a limit order specifies the worst price the investor is willing to accept.

sections.heading: Why stock prices move
paragraphs: Prices change when the balance between willing buyers and sellers changes. New information about earnings, competition, regulation, interest rates or the economy can alter what investors believe a company is worth.
A stock can also move because of broader market sentiment even when the company's underlying business has not changed significantly that day.

sections.heading: Valuation matters
paragraphs: A good company is not automatically a good investment at every price. Investors compare the market value of a business with its expected future profits and cash flows.
Common valuation measures include price-to-earnings ratios, free-cash-flow yields and enterprise-value multiples. Each metric has limitations and should be interpreted in context.

sections.heading: Risk, diversification and time horizon
paragraphs: Individual companies can fail, lose market share or suffer permanent declines. Diversification can reduce dependence on one company but cannot remove broad market risk.
Short-term market moves are difficult to predict consistently. Longer horizons give business fundamentals more time to influence outcomes, but losses are still possible and no return is guaranteed.

faq.question: What happens when I buy a stock?
faq.answer: Your broker executes an order for shares in the market. You then own the economic and legal rights associated with that share class.

faq.question: Why can a stock fall after good earnings?
faq.answer: Markets price expectations in advance. Results can be good in absolute terms but still disappoint compared with what investors expected.

faq.question: Is the stock market the same as the economy?
faq.answer: No. Public companies represent only part of the economy, and stock prices reflect expected future profits as well as current economic conditions.
